_: The connection layer. Maps ingredient names AS PUBLISHED RECIPES WRITE THEM to this kitchen's item ids.
_why: Silvio, 2026-08-12: 'looking for the recipes online is the easy part, I think the hard part is us figuring out how we connect that to what's in the kitchen.' He is right, and this file is that hard part. Recipe corpora and scrapers are commodities: recipe-scrapers handles 649 sites for free, and every serious recipe site publishes JSON-LD because Google requires it for search results. What nobody can sell us is the knowledge that `yellowonion` is his 3 lb bag of yellow, that `whiteonion` is two new ones bought 08-12, that `spaghetti_cooked` is leftovers in the fridge and NOT the dry Barilla in the pantry, and that `beef` is browned and bagged while `beef-raw` is frozen mince. That is what this table holds.
_rules: Longest match wins, so `ground beef` must beat `beef`. The matcher sorts by phrase length before testing.

NEVER alias two things that behave differently into one id. Fresh tomatoes are not tinned tomatoes are not tomato sauce are not tomato paste, and that exact confusion rejected a bolognese on 2026-08-11.
`staple: true` items are assumed present and never counted as missing, because presence is binary and lives in KITCHEN.md rather than the event log.

An unmatched ingredient is reported as UNKNOWN, never as missing. Missing means we know he lacks it; unknown means this table has a gap. Conflating them would silently reject recipes he could cook, which is the failure mode of the whole verbatim experiment.

_knownGaps._: Things published recipes ask for that this kitchen genuinely does not have, listed so the matcher reports them as MISSING with a real name rather than as UNKNOWN. Everything here has been hit by an actual rejected recipe.

WHY THIS ROW COST MORE THAN ANY OTHER: it bundled 32 distinct vegetables under one label, and it was the single largest blocker in the whole corpus at 78 dishes where it was the ONLY thing missing. A category gap cannot be partly satisfied, so buying broccoli unblocked nothing and the note asserting "no broccoli, asparagus..." went on being read as true after both had arrived. Never put a shopping CATEGORY where an ingredient belongs. Plain `lettuce` is deliberately NOT in this bucket either: lettuce is modelled as the `saladmix` stock row, so putting it here would describe the same food twice and the row would win. Named varieties he has never owned (baby gem, romaine) stay here.

_vetoes._: If a parsed ingredient name contains any of these substrings, that item can never match it, whatever the alias table says. This is how a specific qualifier beats a generic phrase it happens to contain.

_gapAliases._: Alias phrases for the known gaps, so a recipe naming one is reported MISSING with a reason rather than UNKNOWN.

_substitutes._: requiredItem -> {have: an itemId he owns, note: what to do and the honest cost}. Reported as HAVE VIA, never as a plain have, because it is a different product doing the same job.

stock.note: One Knorr cube per 2 cups of water, per the box. For cooking purposes this IS stock. It is saltier than fresh and has no body from bones, so go easy on other salt in the dish.

tinned tomatoes.note:
REPOINTED 2026-08-22, from `tomatoes_grape` to `tomatoes_canned`. A 796 ml tin of diced tomatoes is the right stand-in for a 28 oz can of crushed: 796 ml is 26.9 oz, so the quantity is the same tin. Crush them against the pan with the spoon as they cook, or give them a few seconds in the bullet blender first. Diced holds its shape longer, so a sauce made from them stays chunkier unless you break them up.

It pointed at 680 g of clearance grape tomatoes, which were 6 days past their date and had been dropped from availability that morning, so the substitute silently stopped working and Budget Bytes' Bolognese went from needing one thing to needing two. That dish is the example he has raised in three separate sessions. A substitute that depends on the most perishable thing in the kitchen is a substitute that expires; prefer the shelf-stable option where one exists.

self raising flour.note: Plain flour plus baking powder: 2 tsp of baking powder per 150 g of flour, whisked in dry. You have both.

cumin seeds.note: You have ground cumin, not seeds. Use about two thirds as much, and add it later than the recipe says: ground spice burns in seconds where seeds want a minute in hot oil. You lose the pop of a whole seed.

cheddar.note: Monterey Jack, same weight. It melts like a mild cheddar and browns a little paler, so a gratin or a toastie works as written. What you lose is the tang: cheddar is sharp and Jack is not, so in anything where the cheese is the flavour rather than the texture, expect it to taste mild. Adding a little grated parmesan brings some of the sharpness back.

wine and cider vinegar.note: Distilled white vinegar stands in for cider or wine vinegar at a pinch: same job, sharper and flatter, none of the fruit. Fine in a cooked sauce, poor anywhere it is tasted raw.

wholewheat flour.note: Plain all-purpose flour works. Wholewheat carries the bran, so it drinks more liquid and bakes denser and nuttier; swapping white in gives a lighter, softer result. In a muffin where it is a quarter of the flour, barely noticeable.

golden syrup.note: Honey sets a little firmer and tastes of honey, which golden syrup does not. In a flapjack or a chewy bar it works; anything where the syrup is the flavour will taste different.

icing sugar.note: Blitz white sugar in the bullet blender for about 30 seconds, until it looks like flour and no grains are visible. Use the same volume the recipe asks for, measured AFTER blending, because it fluffs up. Let the dust settle before opening the jar. It will not be quite as fine as shop-bought and there is no cornstarch in it, so it thickens an icing slightly less; for dusting a cake it is indistinguishable.

oyster mushrooms.note: Cremini work and taste meatier and less silky. Slice them thicker than the recipe says so they do not disappear into the soup.

ricevinegar.note: You have distilled white vinegar, not rice. It is stronger and has none of rice vinegar's slight sweetness, so use a little less than the recipe says and taste before adding the rest. In a sauce carrying honey or sugar the difference is small; in a dressing or a quick pickle it is the whole flavour.

_notAnIngredient._: Stock ids that are NOT food and must never be counted as invisible to the matcher. This list exists so the check in corpus.ts can be strict by default: anything live in the fold that no alias phrase and no staple can reach is REPORTED on /kitchen/find, unless it is declared here. A new receipt cannot add itself to this list, which is the point.

_shopNotes._: ONE SHORT CLAUSE, for the screen. `_knownGaps` is the agent-facing record and grew into dated incident write-ups, which is right for a repo and wrong for a phone: on 2026-08-22 the shopping surface printed "NARROWED 2026-08-21. BROCCOLI is now its own stock item and is out of this bucket, and asparagus already had its own id. Still missing: green beans..." under a row. His words: "There is so much text here. It does not make sense... so much fluff that does not add value. Just go straight to the point." The UI reads THIS map and nothing else, so the long form cannot leak again by construction. No dates, no history, no capitals. If a gap has nothing worth saying, it gets no entry and the row shows only its name and count. A note that merely lists the same ingredients the row already prints is duplication, not information: eight were removed on 2026-08-22 for exactly that. Keep an entry only where it says something the names cannot.
